Justus
JUS-tus
n. (a surname or Roman name borne by at least three men in the New Testament)
Latin Iustus, just, righteous, upright; a common Roman cognomen adopted by several Jewish and Jewish-Christian men of the apostolic era.

Biblical Definition

Justus is the Latin surname of at least three distinct men in the New Testament, each appearing at a hinge moment in the early church. The first is a candidate to replace Judas among the twelve: “they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias” (Acts 1:23), though the lot fell to Matthias instead (Acts 1:26) — Justus thus stands as a man esteemed worthy of apostleship by the gathered church yet passed over by the LORD’s own sovereign choosing, a sobering pattern for any ambition after office. The second is a Corinthian God-fearer whose house became, after the synagogue’s rejection of Paul’s preaching, the base for the church’s continued work in that city: Paul “entered into a certain man’s house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue” (Acts 18:7), a deliberately provocative proximity that put the new congregation in full view of the old. The third is a Jewish believer among Paul’s few faithful fellow-laborers during a Roman imprisonment: “Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Colossians 4:11) — a man whose given name, Jesus (the same as the Lord’s own, a common Jewish name of the era), Paul quietly passes over in favor of his surname, perhaps out of reverence.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Justus as a common Roman name meaning just or upright; the New Testament names at least three different men who bore it, including a candidate apostle, a Corinthian host, and one of Paul's few faithful companions in prison.

expand to see more

JUSTUS, n. A Latin surname, meaning just or upright, borne by at least three men in the New Testament church.

APOSTLE, n. One sent with a message or commission; specifically, one of the twelve chosen by Christ, or Matthias and Paul added afterward.

LOT, n. That which happens to a person by chance, or which falls to him as his portion; in Scripture, often used to discern God's will.

PROSELYTE, n. A convert; one who worships the true God though not born a Jew, such as many God-fearing Gentiles of Acts.

FELLOWLABORER, n. One who works together with another in a common cause; Paul's term for his faithful companions in ministry.

Key Scripture

Acts 1:23 — "And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias."

Acts 18:7 — "And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man's house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue."

Colossians 4:11 — "And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me."

Acts 1:26 — "And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles."

Modern Corruption

Three unrelated men sharing one common Roman surname, each fitting naturally and without confusion into a different, historically plausible setting, is the texture of real record-keeping, not a symbol invented for literary effect.

expand to see more

Literary-critical readings eager to flatten distinct historical persons into symbolic types miss that Luke and Paul, writing independently, each use Justus as an ordinary contemporary Roman surname attached to ordinary, differentiated men — ancient Jewish adoption of Latin names under Roman rule is well attested outside Scripture, and the casual, non-explanatory way each Justus is introduced argues for straightforward historical reportage rather than deliberate literary patterning.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the Acts 1 Justus especially: being esteemed worthy of the highest visible office in the church by the gathered assembly is not the same as being the LORD's chosen instrument for it, and a man can be genuinely just, genuinely qualified, and still passed over by sovereign appointment — a needed corrective to any ministry culture that equates human esteem with divine calling.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin Iustus, just, righteous, upright; Greek dikaios (G1342), just, righteous; kleros (G2819), lot, portion; sunergos (G4904), fellow-worker.

expand to see more

Latin Iustus — just, righteous, upright; a common Roman cognomen.

Greek dikaios (G1342) — just, righteous; the underlying moral sense the Latin name translates.

Greek kleros (G2819) — lot, portion, inheritance; the means by which Matthias, not Justus, was chosen.

Greek sunergos (G4904) — fellow-worker; Paul's title for the Justus of Colossians 4:11.

Greek sebomai (G4576) — to worship, revere; describing the Corinthian Justus's devotion to God.

Usage

"“Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus” — the candidate passed over for Matthias."

"“A certain man's house, named Justus... whose house joined hard to the synagogue” — the Corinthian host."

"“Jesus, which is called Justus... my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God” — Paul's faithful companion in prison."
